newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition sets sights on state media.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition sets sights on state media.

text.p: Serbia's opposition, flushed with victory, is now setting its sights on wresting control of the media from authoritarian President Slobodan Milosevic as it steps up its struggle for more democracy.

With confidence high after forcing the government finally to admit it lost control of Serbia's biggest cities, including Belgrade, in local elections last November, the opposition wants to chip away at one of the main pillars of Milosevic's power.

Vesna Pesic, co-leader of the Zajedno opposition alliance that has organised daily street protests since those elections, said the reinstatement of the election results was only "the first round in our fight".

Another opposition leader, Zoran Djindjic, said on Tuesday: "A whole range of problems which have been opened in these 8 5 days have not yet even been touched, let alone resolved...our protests call for media freedom, dialogue between the authorities and opposition, and a normalisation of political life in Serbia."
"We want full media freedom, but I'm afraid we shall be seeing each other for quite some time in the fight for this goal," he told the independent Radio Index.

Zajedno was forced to bring its message directly to the streets largely because it was being ignored or distorted by the state-owned media under the president's control, particularly Serbian state television (RTS).

With a handful of independent newspapers and magazines largely confined to Serbia's urban intelligentsia, the television is virtually the only source of information for the majority of the population living in villages and small towns.
It was mainly the fear of losing control of regional media outlets that prompted the government to annul the results of the local elections, claiming unspecified irregularities in voting.

The power of RTS to misinform was illustrated recently when rural supporters of Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party bused into Belgrade for a rally to counter the Zajedno protests told reporters they had no idea people had been demonstrating for weeks, or about the issues.

The importance the ruling party attaches to maintaining its media monopoly was made dramatically clear earlier this year when it sent in police to occupy the radio station in an industrial town where the opposition gained control.

After street violence and a stand-off, a court earlier this month awarded control of the local radio and television station in Kragujevac, south of Belgrade, to the new opposition-led council. The local media in another major city, Nis, is also under opposition control.
Signs of dissension have also started emerging from the once-solid bloc of the state-controlled media.
Last month the main afternoon daily Vercenji Novosti, once slavishly pro-government, stepped up its coverage of the daily street protests with strikingly neutral reporting.

Two weeks ago the private television station BK owned by Serbian magnate Bogoljub Karic, which had studiously ignored the opposition protests, provided graphic pictures of heavy-handed police action against demonstrators.

The aggrieved government threatened to cut off the station's access to state television's transmission network, a favourable deal granted to BK TV because of its previous support for the government which enables it to reach some 60 percent of the country, because it had not paid its dues.
According to local media reports , Karic forcefully reminded RTS that its debt with a Serbian bank he owns was far higher than his TV station's, and the threat was dropped.
